title: Neither coming nor going (section 29)
hook: the Tathagata neither comes nor goes; that is why he is called the Tathagata

segments.voice: Yesterday, merit not held: the bodhisattva gains merit and doesn't take hold of it. Your line: not held.

A map app runs on two questions. Where are you? Where are you going? A blue dot, a line, a time to arrival, and at the end a cheerful voice: you have arrived. A few minutes later, a new destination. Whole days can be lived inside that blue dot, always on the way, rarely there. The Diamond Sutra opened with the Buddha on the move, walking into town for alms and back again. Now, near the end, section twenty-nine seems to erase the whole walk.
screen: `WHERE ARE YOU? WHERE TO?` → `YOU HAVE ARRIVED. AGAIN.` → `THE WALK, ERASED?`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells Subhuti, in paraphrase: if anyone says the Tathagata comes or goes, or stands, or sits, or lies down, that person hasn't understood what I teach. Those are the ordinary shapes of a body's day, and the Tathagata isn't to be pinned to any of them. But we watched him do every one. Back in section one he walked to town with his bowl, ate, came back, washed his feet and sat down. The sutra isn't taking that back. The body walked. The question is whether the one called Tathagata is that walking. The sutra's reason: the Tathagata doesn't go anywhere and doesn't come from anywhere, and that is exactly why he is called the Tathagata. The sutra hands the title its own meaning. Not a traveler who arrived somewhere special, not a visitor who will one day leave. What the name points to was never on the road. It's the cut from the verse about form and sound, one step deeper: not the body's shape, and not its movements either. So much of a life is spent in transit, in the head if not on the road. Almost there. Not yet. Next. Section twenty-nine doesn't tell anyone to stop walking. The dishes still need doing and the bus still leaves at eight. It points at something in the middle of all the walking that isn't going anywhere.
screen: `COMES, GOES, STANDS, SITS, LIES DOWN.` · `BUT WE WATCHED HIM WALK.` · `GOES NOWHERE, COMES FROM NOWHERE.` · `STILL IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WALK.` · then, large: `NEITHER COMING NOR GOING.`

segments.voice: Notice where your mind is headed: the next task, tonight, tomorrow, the blue dot moving. Then let the destination go for a moment; the breath comes, the breath goes, and the knowing of it stays right here. If the mind leaves for somewhere, notice it went, and come back without scolding.
Neither coming nor going. Section twenty-nine: the Tathagata goes nowhere and comes from nowhere, and that is why he is called the Tathagata. Today's word.
Your line: neither coming nor going. Nowhere this breath has to take you. Day one thousand one hundred forty-six, and you're right here.

howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists who study the Diamond Sutra read section 29 as the sutra's own gloss on the title Tathagata.

chat.says: The Diamond Sutra shows the Buddha walking to town. So why say he neither comes nor goes?
options: The body walked; the sutra says the one called Tathagata goes nowhere and comes from nowhere.
Because the walk in section one never happened; the sutra admits it was made up.
Because after awakening, the Buddha stopped moving and only sat in meditation.
chat.meaning: Section twenty-nine doesn't take back the walk; it says the Tathagata isn't pinned to coming or going, which is why he has that name.
